title: How Long Do You Spend Grading Articles of the Week?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart answers the common objection that Kelly Gallagher's weekly article-of-the-week assignment buries teachers in 100 to 200 pages of grading. His answer is that he spends roughly four seconds per response, and that Gallagher does the same, because the assignment's purpose is reading, reflecting and knowing more about the world rather than producing gradable summative writing. From this he derives the principle that purpose dictates grading. He lists reasons rapid grading is defensible: the goal is to inform, slow grading does not reliably improve writers, modeling with student exemplars beats nitpicky comments, and the volume only works if grading is quick. He closes by giving teachers permission to grade smarter, while admitting he is not refusing to grade at all.
points: Purpose dictates grading: when the point of an assignment is volume of reading and reflection, time-intensive scoring defeats the purpose.
Quick grading is presented as the only way an article-of-the-week routine is humanly possible alongside the rest of the curriculum.
Whole-class modeling with strong student examples from the previous week moves writing further than individualized nitpicky comments.
Gallagher's test of enough volume is that students should read and write far more than any teacher could grade.
The piece reframes teacher guilt about grading as a misconception that can trap teachers in unsustainable routines.
quotes: Most weeks I spend about 4 seconds grading each article of the week response Sounds like malpractice, right? But if it's malpractice, I'm in good company.

Remember: the primary purpose of AoWs is to help our kids know more about the world than our curricula will cover. AoWs are one way we try flooding our students with opportunities to read, write, and think.

Too often, we lose sight of the “why” behind an assignment or an instructional move, and this causes us hours of wasted effort. Anything done with a lack of clear purpose is bound to collect problems like a snowball collects snow on its way down a mountain.

Because modeling and feedback are far better at moving writers than nitpicky grading. My students improve their writing far more through my use of several solid student examples from last week's AoW than they do through my nitpicky comments. Feedback doesn't always need to be individualized to be effective.

The point here isn't to refuse to grade things; [2] the point is to grade purposefully. Grading must serve our long-term purposes, and our long-term purposes must not be circumvented by our own guilt-inducing misconceptions about grading
